title: Hash maps
summary: Key lookup is O(1) on average and O(n) when every key collides.

parts.rule: Average lookup, insert, and delete by key are constant time when the hash spreads keys. The worst case collapses toward linear when every key lands in one bucket.
parts.why: Counting, grouping, and "have I seen this before" show up constantly. A map turns those scans into expected constant probes. Interviewers still want you to admit the collision story so you do not claim a hard O(1) guarantee the table cannot keep.
parts.example: SAMPLE: you count character frequencies in a short phrase. For each character you bump a map entry. Reporting the tallest count then walks the map once. If a pathological hash sent every character to one chain, that walk and those bumps would behave like a list — so you mention average versus worst when you quote the cost.
parts.use: Reach for a hash map when keys are not dense integers, when you need membership or aggregation by arbitrary identity, or when you trade a little memory for fewer full scans. Pair it with a list when you must also preserve insertion order.
parts.refuse: Refuse a hash map when you need sorted keys or range queries; a tree map or a sorted array fits better. Refuse it as the only structure when memory is tight and the key space is a compact integer range that an array could index directly. Refuse claiming worst-case constant time unless the prompt gives a perfect hash.

body:
Rule. Average lookup, insert, and delete by key are constant time when the hash spreads keys. The worst case collapses toward linear when every key lands in one bucket.

Why it matters. Counting, grouping, and "have I seen this before" show up constantly. A map turns those scans into expected constant probes. Interviewers still want you to admit the collision story so you do not claim a hard O(1) guarantee the table cannot keep.

SAMPLE example. SAMPLE: you count character frequencies in a short phrase. For each character you bump a map entry. Reporting the tallest count then walks the map once. If a pathological hash sent every character to one chain, that walk and those bumps would behave like a list — so you mention average versus worst when you quote the cost.

When to use. Reach for a hash map when keys are not dense integers, when you need membership or aggregation by arbitrary identity, or when you trade a little memory for fewer full scans. Pair it with a list when you must also preserve insertion order.

When to refuse. Refuse a hash map when you need sorted keys or range queries; a tree map or a sorted array fits better. Refuse it as the only structure when memory is tight and the key space is a compact integer range that an array could index directly. Refuse claiming worst-case constant time unless the prompt gives a perfect hash.
